subject: research/interleave-twin
professional: a communications/coding-theory researcher (burst-error channels, ARQ/FEC design) reviewing for a networking or robotics-comms venue

evidence.correctness: Ran `PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py` and diffed against experiments/results.txt: identical. Recomputed independently in /usr/bin/python3.13 with numpy, building the 2-state transition matrix and using matrix_power (not the author's closed form for lag-g): real residual of 5 back-to-back copies at lam=0.8 = 0.099574 (reported 0.0996), lam=0.3 0.007496 (0.0075), lam=0.9 0.14328 (0.143); copies needed at g=1 for lam=0.3/0.5/0.7/0.8/0.9 = 8/12/21/32/65 (reported same); lam=0.8 D=48: 4 copies g=16 gives 2.2036e-3 and 49 consecutive 4.639e-5 (reported 2.2e-3, 4.64e-5); brute-force min-latency design over (r<=8, g<600): (12,7,2), (35,8,5), (77,8,11), (154,8,22) as reported. Separate vectorised numpy Monte Carlo (2e6 chains, different RNG and construction) for lam=0.8, r=3, g=3: 0.07437 vs exact 0.07432. All numbers reproduce. The floor claim (r<=4 infeasible since p^4=1.6e-3 > 1e-3) is correct by q_g>=p. Capped at 3 because the model is a closed form for a toy chain; the numbers are right for the model stated.
evidence.completeness: README/whitepaper claims checked: (1) twin design r=5 and real residuals/ratios: works, matches results.txt; (2) two-copy ratio 1+lam^g(1-p)/p and g=6/17/36: works; (3) copy-budget min-latency table: works; (4) fixed-deadline counter-case: works; (5) Monte Carlo agreement: works (max 2.06 se, README says 0.4 to 2.1); 10 tests 'under 1 s': true; run.py 'about 1 s': true; Live page link not loaded (no network check) but the build registers the project (research/_audit/audit.json lists it). experiments/figure.py and residual_vs_lam.svg exist. No stubs or TODOs found. Whitepaper 'Next steps' are clearly future work.
evidence.verification: `cd research/interleave-twin; PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` -> Ran 10 tests, OK. Mutation 1: q_lag changed to lam**(g+1): 4 tests failed (caught). Mutation 2: copies_needed_real `1 +` -> `2 +`: test_copies_needed failed (caught). Both reverted; git status clean, tests OK again. (A stale __pycache__ briefly made a post-revert run fail, an artefact of same-second mtimes, cleared by deleting __pycache__; not a repo defect.) Gaps: no test pins results.txt to run.py output (the headline table could drift), no test of figure.py, no input-validation tests; the Monte Carlo and enumeration tests only validate the closed form against the same model assumptions (circularity inherent to a model-vs-model study).
evidence.craft: Read src/interleave_twin/model.py (94 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, figure.py (imports only; does not use research/_shared/linefig.py as research/CLAUDE.md suggests). Code is clean, short and documented. Defects: no input validation: residual_real(0.2,-0.5,2,1) returns -0.04 (a negative probability; lam is documented in [0,1) but not enforced); best_spacing_for_deadline(p,lam,D,1) raises ZeroDivisionError; residual_real with g=0 silently returns p*q^(r-1) with q_0=1 (all copies in one slot) without complaint; best_design silently returns None past g_max=400 (checked: lam=0.99 r<=8 still finds (763,8,109), so ok in the tested range, but 'infeasible' in the table can mean 'beyond g_max'). best_spacing_for_deadline assumes uniform spacing without noting it is not proven optimal for fixed r and D.
evidence.claims: Every number in README and whitepaper checked against experiments/results.txt: all match (23x/81x/208x/311x/448x, 8/12/21/32/65, 4.2 and 1.28 ratios, g=6/17/36, 12/35/77/154, 4.6e-5 vs 2.2e-3). Disclaimers present (Stylised: simulated link, no radio traces, all-or-nothing loss, known stationary params). Prior work is cited (Gilbert 1960, Elliott 1963, Lin & Costello 2004) and the README is honest that repetition/interleaving against burst errors is classical. Issue: the 'Builds on' line leans on ARPG/RECUV 'directions' with no paper reproduced (disclosed as such). Minor overreach: the README headline presents 'send repeats back to back is wrong on a bursty link' as a finding when it is textbook; the whitepaper title says 'what spacing buys' without noting the classical result. Whitepaper statement 'At D=3 spacing does not help (0.119 for r=4, same as consecutive)' is true because g=1 at D=3,r=4.
evidence.fitness: Research use: a researcher could use the closed form p*q_g^(r-1) and the design tables as a teaching baseline, but it is a toy: the 'real' link is another simulated model of the same family as the twin, so the study shows sensitivity to a chosen model, not a measured twin-to-real gap. No radio trace, no estimation of (p, lam) from data, no ARQ/FEC comparison, no copy-induced load. Nearest prior work: Gilbert-Elliott burst channels with repetition codes and block interleaving (Lin & Costello; Ebert/Willig and Yajnik et al. 1999 on measured packet-loss correlation and FEC spacing; Bolot et al. 1999 on FEC vs loss correlation for audio); the P(all r copies lost)=p*q_g^(r-1) identity is a direct Markov-chain computation. The result is sound but not new; the new part is only the framing as a twin-certification gap for multi-robot map updates. Nothing here is publishable as a standalone paper, and the programme bar in research/CLAUDE.md (PhD-level, real data) is not met. Companion in structure to dropout-twin, which uses the same chain and p*q^(m-1) form.
evidence.domain: A networking/coding researcher would first ask: is the loss correlation realistic and measured, and why use blind repetition rather than FEC (k-of-n erasure codes) or ARQ? The method matches textbook Gilbert/Elliott analysis and the exponential decay lam^g is correct for a 2-state chain. Departures: Gilbert (1960) allows loss in the good state (the code uses the degenerate all-or-nothing case, so 'lam' is the only free parameter and the Elliott soft-loss case is absent); fixed-spacing repetition is a dominated scheme versus erasure coding, which is listed as next step only; no latency-vs-load analysis of the copies on a shared channel; no empirical lam values from radio literature to justify the 0.3 to 0.95 range. The fixed-deadline counter-case (4) is a useful honest caveat, but it compares designs with different copy counts (r=D+1 vs r=4), so it is partly a copy-budget statement rather than a spacing statement.

defects.what: Headline finding (independent-loss twin underestimates repetition-coding residual on a bursty link; spacing helps) is classical (Gilbert-Elliott/interleaving, Yajnik 1999, Bolot 1999) and the 'real' link is simulated, so the work is not new and is not validated against any trace; prior work is cited generically but not these loss-correlation/FEC papers
Blind repetition is compared only to itself; erasure coding or ARQ, the practitioner's alternatives, are deferred to Next steps, so the design advice has no baseline a comms engineer would accept
No input validation: lam<0 returns a negative 'probability'; r=1 in best_spacing_for_deadline raises ZeroDivisionError; g=0 silently accepted
No test pins experiments/results.txt to run.py output, so the headline table can drift from code without a failing test
best_spacing_for_deadline assumes equal gaps; optimality for fixed r and D is not shown, and the fixed-deadline counter-case compares unequal copy counts
figure.py does not use the shared research/_shared/linefig.py helper

verdict: The arithmetic is right: every reported number reproduced from an independent matrix-power implementation, a brute-force design search and a separate 2e6-chain Monte Carlo, results.txt regenerates byte-identically, and two seeded mutations (a lag exponent and an off-by-one in the copy count) were caught by the 10 tests. The README claims are all backed by results.txt and carry honest 'Stylised' limits. But the finding itself is a textbook consequence of the Gilbert-Elliott model (burst loss defeats back-to-back repetition, spacing restores independence at lam^g) and the 'real' link is another simulation, so it is sound but not new, uses no radio data, and omits the practitioner's actual alternatives (erasure codes, ARQ). By the rubric it meets the bar (correctness, claims, verification all 3; median of the seven is 3) but fitness and domain are 2: a good teaching-note-level sensitivity study, not PhD-level research. Worst defect: novelty and external validity (classical result, simulated reality, no comparison to FEC/ARQ).
